definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that shows they have the same structure or pattern.
definitions.example: Like a map of a subway system that has the same connections as the real tracks, even though the map looks different.

definitions.definition: A Latin phrase meaning 'end of itself' or 'self-termination'; here it refers to a closed system's inability to complete or validate itself.
definitions.example: Like a calculator that can't check if its own answer is correct without an outside person.

definitions.definition: A system that does not exchange matter, energy, or information with anything outside itself.
definitions.example: A sealed jar with a plant and soil, where nothing goes in or out.

definitions.definition: The property of a system that cannot prove all true statements about itself from within its own rules.
definitions.example: Like a game where you can't prove the final score using only the rules of the game itself.

definitions.definition: To prove that your own rules or statements are correct without help from outside.
definitions.example: Like a student grading their own test and claiming they got 100% without a teacher checking.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; in physics, it always increases in a closed system.
definitions.example: Like a messy room that gets messier over time if you never clean it.

definitions.definition: A situation where the cost or burden is not shared equally; one side pays all or most of the cost.
definitions.example: Like a friend paying for your lunch without asking you to pay them back.

definitions.definition: Not based on how good or deserving something or someone is.
definitions.example: Like a lottery win that you get just by chance, not because you earned it.

definitions.definition: Existing or happening before something else in time.
definitions.example: Like the rain that falls before the grass grows.

definitions.definition: An action by God that changes the normal course of events.
definitions.example: Like a story where a character is saved by a miracle at the last moment.

definitions.definition: Two famous proofs showing that any system of math strong enough to do basic arithmetic cannot prove all true statements about itself, and cannot prove its own consistency.
definitions.example: Like a rulebook that can't prove that the rulebook itself has no contradictions.

definitions.definition: A proof that no formal language can define what 'true' means within that same language; you need a bigger language outside it.
definitions.example: Like a dictionary that can't define the word 'dictionary' without using another dictionary.

definitions.definition: A proof that no computer program can always correctly predict whether another program will eventually stop or run forever.
definitions.example: Like trying to write a program that can tell if any other program will crash — it's impossible.

definitions.definition: The law that says in an isolated system, disorder (entropy) always increases or stays the same; it never decreases on its own.
definitions.example: Like an ice cube melting in a warm room — it never unmelts by itself.

definitions.definition: A principle stating that erasing one bit of information in a computer always produces a tiny amount of heat; information processing has a minimum energy cost.
definitions.example: Like how deleting a file on your laptop makes the computer slightly warmer.

definitions.definition: An argument that everything that exists could have not existed (is contingent), so there must be something that must exist (is necessary) to explain why anything exists at all.
definitions.example: Like a chain of dominoes — each one falls because the one before it fell, but there must be a first push to start the chain.

definitions.definition: Something that could have been different or could have not existed at all.
definitions.example: Like the color of your shirt — it could have been blue instead of red.

definitions.definition: Something that must exist and cannot not exist; necessary.
definitions.example: Like the number 2 — it has to exist in math; you can't have a math where 2 doesn't exist.

definitions.definition: Logically consistent; not self-contradictory.
definitions.example: Like a story where all the details fit together without contradictions.

definitions.definition: A combination of statements joined by 'and'; all parts must be true for the whole to be true.
definitions.example: Like saying 'it is raining AND it is cold' — both must be true.

definitions.definition: The property of coming from outside a system, not from within.
definitions.example: Like a rescue team that comes from outside a collapsed building.

definitions.definition: The property of being enough or complete; not needing anything else.
definitions.example: Like having a full tank of gas for a road trip — you don't need to stop for more.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse that says salvation is a gift from God, not something earned by good deeds, so no one can boast.
definitions.example: Like receiving a birthday present you didn't work for.

definitions.definition: A number that measures how strongly two systems are connected or influence each other.
definitions.example: Like a volume knob that controls how much sound comes from a speaker to your ears.

definitions.definition: A value that measures how independent or self-governing a system is; here, u=1 means fully closed, u=0 means fully open.
definitions.example: Like a dimmer switch for a light — higher means more self-contained, lower means more open to outside influence.

definitions.definition: The process of making a system logically consistent or orderly again after it has become disordered or contradictory.
definitions.example: Like untangling a knotted necklace so it becomes a smooth chain again.

definitions.definition: The study of how parts of a system are connected and arranged, ignoring exact sizes or distances.
definitions.example: Like a map of a city's subway lines showing which stations connect, not how far apart they are.

definitions.definition: A belief that humans can save themselves by their own efforts without God's help.
definitions.example: Like thinking you can lift yourself off the ground by pulling on your own shoelaces.

definitions.definition: A belief that humans can start the process of salvation on their own, and God finishes it.
definitions.example: Like thinking you can push a car a little bit and then God pushes it the rest of the way.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical machine that runs forever without any new energy input; impossible because of the laws of thermodynamics.
definitions.example: Like a fan that spins forever without being plugged in or having batteries.

definitions.definition: A test that checks whether two things can be exchanged without changing the meaning or result.
definitions.example: Like checking if swapping the salt and sugar in a recipe gives the same taste — it doesn't.

definitions.definition: A mapping where each item in one set matches exactly one item in another set, and no two items match the same thing.
definitions.example: Like assigning each student a unique locker number — no two students share a locker.

definitions.definition: Not repeated or unnecessary; each part adds something new.
definitions.example: Like a list of ingredients where each one is needed for the recipe — no duplicates.

definitions.definition: A limitation on what a system can prove or know about itself, based on Gödel's theorems.
definitions.example: Like a computer that can't check if its own operating system has a virus without help from an outside program.

definitions.definition: The challenge of making sure an AI system's goals match what humans actually want, not just what it was told.
definitions.example: Like telling a robot to 'clean the room' and it throws away everything, including your phone, because you didn't say 'don't throw away valuables'.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation — how people are saved or rescued from sin and its consequences.
definitions.example: Like different theories about how a person can be saved in a religious context.

definitions.definition: A problem or malfunction in a system; something that goes wrong.
definitions.example: Like a crack in a bridge that makes it unsafe.

definitions.definition: A 16th-century movement that led to the creation of Protestant churches, focusing on salvation by faith alone.
definitions.example: Like a big change in how people thought about church and salvation in the 1500s.

definitions.definition: The belief that salvation comes only through trust in God, not by doing good works.
definitions.example: Like believing that a gift is received just by accepting it, not by paying for it.

definitions.definition: The belief that salvation requires both trust in God and doing good deeds.
definitions.example: Like thinking you need both a key and a password to open a door.

definitions.definition: Going both ways; information or influence flows in two directions.
definitions.example: Like a two-way street where cars can go both east and west.

definitions.definition: The act of proving a statement or theory wrong by showing a counterexample.
definitions.example: Like showing that the statement 'all swans are white' is false by finding a black swan.

definitions.definition: Based on self-evident truths (axioms) that are assumed without proof.
definitions.example: Like starting a math problem with 'let x = 5' — you don't prove it, you just assume it.

definitions.definition: Things that are easily observed or obvious, as opposed to deeper underlying causes.
definitions.example: Like seeing a leaf float on water (surface) without knowing about the water currents underneath.

definitions.definition: A book by Leibniz that argues reality is made of simple, indivisible units called monads.
definitions.example: Like a theory that everything is built from tiny, unbreakable building blocks that have their own inner life.

definitions.definition: A theoretical field in the Theophysics framework that represents the fundamental substrate of reality, often associated with information and coherence.
definitions.example: Like an invisible ocean of potential that underlies everything, similar to how a magnetic field surrounds a magnet.

definitions.definition: The limit beyond which a closed system cannot go in terms of self-knowledge or self-validation, as defined by Gödel's theorems.
definitions.example: Like a fence that marks the edge of what a system can figure out about itself without outside help.
